pages.text: Joyce was reading a magazine when she shouted, “Listen! In Kigali, the capital of Rwanda, everyone cleans the streets together on the last Saturday of every month!” Pelpuo looked up from his lunch. “Everyone? Even the president?” “Even the president,” said Joyce. “It is called umuganda, and it means coming together.”

“Everyone?
Even the president?” “Even the president,” said Joyce.
“It is called umuganda, and it means coming together.”
pages.alt: A girl holds up a magazine while a boy listens, with a picture of people sweeping a street.

pages.text: Madam Tagoe came over. “Umuganda was made national in 1995,” she said. “On the last Saturday of the month, people take part in community work for about three hours, starting around eight o’clock. Cleaning is one job, but they also build roads, repair homes and plant gardens. The local people decide what to do.”

pages.alt: People of all ages sweep a road and plant a garden together on a bright morning.

pages.text: “There is more,” said Madam Tagoe. “In 2008, Rwanda banned single-use plastic bags. Carrying one could bring a fine. Many households separate their waste, and private companies collect it for a fee. Together these things helped Kigali become known as one of the cleanest cities in Africa.”

pages.alt: A market stall wrapping goods in paper and cloth bags instead of plastic bags.

pages.text: “Is it all perfect?” asked Pelpuo. “No,” said Madam Tagoe. “Some people call umuganda forced labour, because people who do not take part can be fined. Some shopkeepers lose business on those mornings. Two sources even disagree about who must take part: one says people from eighteen to sixty-five, another says sixteen to sixty-five. A fair student writes down all of that.”

pages.text: “What about us?” asked Joyce. “Ghana has had a monthly National Sanitation Day,” said Madam Tagoe. “A proposed law once suggested making it compulsory, and it was argued over. Some people said the law would help. Others said it was not fair to force people. What do you think?” Pelpuo grinned. “I think the broom is mightier than the bill.”

pages.text: The class held a vote. Some wanted a rule. Some wanted a choice. In the end, they agreed on a plan: a Last Saturday Club, open to everyone, voluntary, with a snack for those who came. Each month they would clean one gutter, one bus stop and one corner of the market, with adults doing the dangerous work.

pages.alt: Pupils raise their hands and a poster reads: Last Saturday Club.

pages.text: On the first Last Saturday, thirty-two people came. There were pupils, parents, a trader, a taxi driver, a pastor and an imam. They filled sixty-one bags with rubbish. Pelpuo counted the bags and the sachets in each. “Eighteen sachets in one bag,” he said. “Eighteen small blockers that did not end up in the gutter.”

pages.alt: A crowd of children and adults with brooms and sacks cleaning a road, smiling in the sun.

pages.text: At the end of the morning, Joyce stood on a crate. “Rwanda did it with rules and with community spirit,” she said. “We have our rules, but we also need our spirit. And we need leaders to do their part too.” Everyone clapped. Madam Tagoe wrote the next date on the board: the last Saturday of next month. The end.
